teaser: A reply to Nadzeya Stalbouskaya: removing servers simplifies only if you move to real commodities, so map it and ask who would certify it.
core_idea: Removing your own servers and databases can outsource complexity rather than remove it, so the move must be a conscious, mapped decision: moving a component to a genuine commodity such as passkeys or object storage simplifies, while a young startup's service may only look like a commodity, and the test is whether anyone would certify, insure or guarantee what you now depend on.

quotes.text: If the answer is nobody, you have not simplified.

figures.caption: The thread on LinkedIn, 25 October 2026: my reply to Stephan Bitton, that my strategy has been to have no databases, run serverless services and now no server-side code I maintain, and Nadzeya Stalbouskaya's challenge: removing databases and server-side code does not necessarily remove complexity; sometimes it moves it into external services we do not fully control. "How do you distinguish between genuinely simplifying architecture and simply outsourcing its complexity?"

Three moves to the right, mapped: our own login, with passwords, resets and a password database, moved to passkeys, which every major browser and platform supports; our own database server, with on-call, failover and upgrades, moved to object storage and static hosting; and our own version of a feature moved to a young startup's service, which looks like a commodity on our map but rests on its own early code and its own suppliers. Positions are illustrative.

Maturity is what can be certified, insured and held to an SLA: explorer, genesis and custom, glued together, which nobody should certify or will insure; villager, product, which works and is used, certifiable in parts, where SG/Send sits; town planner, commodity and utility, stable by design, documented, with a track record and high SLAs, where passkeys sit. Rising with maturity: security, stability, reliability, disaster recovery, resilience, documentation, SLAs, insurability and certifiability.
